title: Webb visits a star-forming spiral
caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 2283, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 2283 · constellation Canis Major · about 45 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #45 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Puffy, patchy clouds of gas and dust fill this close, nearly face-on view of a spiral galaxy, glowing red, orange and yellow and brightest at the center and along two winding arms. This is NGC 2283, a barred spiral about 45 million light-years away in Canis Major, seen by Webb's NIRCam and MIRI.

Six snapshots through different near- and mid-infrared filters, adding up to 17 minutes, went into the picture. They show the galaxy's stars, hydrogen clouds heated by young stars, and sooty molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. Dense knots of gas lit by young stars trace the arms, evidence that cold hydrogen is being turned into new stars.

Galaxies like this often host core-collapse supernovae. On 28 January 2023, one named SN 2023AXU was discovered here. Such explosions can fling gas across hundreds of light-years, enriching star-forming clouds with elements like oxygen and sodium that later end up in new stars.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.22 x 2.07 arcminutes) and distance (45 million light years), the frame spans roughly 29,000 × 27,000 light-years. Its light set out about 45 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam and MIRI combined near- and mid-infrared light. Blue marks starlight and hydrogen emission, green and orange intermediate filters including PAH emission, and red the longest mid-infrared filters.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the human eye.

explore: SN 2023AXU is a Type II supernova, which happens when a star with at least eight times the Sun's mass has its core collapse. The observations belong to program #3707, which covers 55 nearby star-forming galaxies. The large, bright stars with diffraction spikes are in our own Milky Way, between us and NGC 2283.
alt: A nearly face-on spiral galaxy full of patchy red, orange and yellow clouds of gas and dust, brightest at the center and along two arms, with a few large bright white foreground stars.
